From Humble Homes to Built Heritage

Dakota

Saving Dakota Crescent — the case of an ageing estate, a citizens' campaign, and an impossible choice.

Scroll to begin
This site adapts From Humble Homes to Built Heritage: The Case of Saving Dakota Crescent, a case study by LKYSPP's Case Insights Unit, for interactive use in this workshop.
A question to hold onto

Every year, ageing public housing estates across Singapore make way for redevelopment — almost always quietly. This one didn't. As you read, keep asking: what made Dakota Crescent different?

1958Built by the Singapore Improvement Trust

One of the last of its kind

The Singapore Improvement Trust — a colonial-era body set up in 1927 to modernise the city's infrastructure — built Dakota Crescent in 1958. It was one of the Trust's last projects before it was dissolved in 1960 and folded into a brand-new agency: the Housing and Development Board.

Dakota Crescent in 1965 — just a few years old at the time, and still relatively new.

Seventeen low-rise blocks were arranged around a shared courtyard, including eight distinctive curved “butterfly” blocks and a dove-shaped playground that became one of the last surviving heritage playgrounds in the country.

By the 2010s, the estate housed several hundred rental households under the HDB Public Rental Scheme — the large majority elderly, low-income tenants, many of whom had lived there since it opened.

Four typologies, one estate

A unique and thoughtful design

Dakota Crescent was planned as a self-contained estate: 2- to 7-storey blocks arranged around open lawns and communal spaces, with a varied, deliberately climate-responsive design rather than a single repeated block type.

Blocks were oriented to catch prevailing winds and avoid direct sun — a climate-conscious approach, not just a formal one. Wide grass patches and voids between blocks were a deliberate planning feature too, giving residents light, ventilation, and informal play areas long before today's community parks.

The estate's most famous typology — curved “butterfly” or “pi-shaped” blocks, their two wings folding toward a shared courtyard.

The estate actually held four distinct block typologies, not one. Straight slab blocks like Block 10 kept things simple — regular balconies and windows opening onto the lawns. The seven-storey butterfly blocks broke that monotony, their curved plan maximising privacy and forming semi-enclosed courtyards. Low walk-ups like Block 24 were staircase-served, three to four storeys, with pitched red roofs. And two-storey shophouse-style blocks like Block 12 put shops on the ground floor beneath the flats above — a small slice of commercial life woven into a residential estate.

Architect Jonathan Poh, who would later lead the campaign to save the estate, pointed out that two of Dakota Crescent's butterfly blocks echoed a style once found in Whampoa and Queenstown — both long since demolished. By the 2010s, Dakota Crescent held the last surviving examples of that architecture anywhere in Singapore.

Not every block was a dramatic butterfly wing — this modest two-storey block represents a different typology again.
Block 18 — one of Dakota Crescent's curved “butterfly” blocks.
What the estate held

A slower way of living

Physically modest — plain brick and concrete, open corridors, generous green space — the estate's charm lay less in grandeur than in what it preserved: a closely-knit, communal way of life increasingly rare in high-rise Singapore.

This wasn't just a happy accident of old age and slower times — the architecture actively produced it. The same wide voids and grass patches built in for light and ventilation doubled as informal play areas and gathering spots; the same low-rise, open-corridor layout that saved on construction cost also put neighbours within easy earshot and eyeline of each other. Long-time residents knew each other by name, left their doors open, and gathered in shared corridors and courtyards. This social fabric, as much as the architecture that enabled it, is what heritage advocates and former residents alike would later describe having lost.

Before the notice ever arrived

How Singapore re-develops

By the time HDB's development notice reached Dakota Crescent in 2014, the institutional machinery that produced it had been running for decades.

When HDB took over from the SIT in 1960, it inherited a young nation's most urgent problem: a severe housing shortage. Its mandate was — and remains — to house a growing population at scale, on an island with almost no land to spare. Its newer, denser estates became the story Singapore told about its own progress; the older, SIT-built blocks that came before, Dakota Crescent among them, registered less prominently in public memory, even as they sat on increasingly valuable, centrally-located land.

Dakota Crescent was a case in point: wedged between Mountbatten and Dakota MRT stations (both completed only in 2010, decades newer than the estate itself), close to the city centre and several established schools, it occupied exactly the kind of central, well-connected site HDB's intensification mission is built to unlock — the BTO project eventually launched on part of the land drew buyer interest specifically for that mature-estate location.

The intensification is literal: Dakota Crescent's blocks topped out at seven storeys, but the new development rising on part of the site runs 17 to 22 storeys — two to three times the height, meaning several times as many households can now be housed on the same footprint of land.

The state's ability to act on land like this was formalised early: the Land Acquisition Act (1966, amended 1973) gave it broad power to assemble sites at controlled cost. Two recurring planning documents route which sites get redeveloped and when — the Concept Plan, revisited roughly once a decade for long-term land use, and the Master Plan, a five-year statutory plan for the medium term.

The “conservation dilemma”

Urban studies scholars Kong and Yeoh (1994) describe Singapore as caught between two pressures at once: the drive to modernise and renew, and the need to reclaim its own urban heritage as a shared, collective past. Dakota Crescent would become one of the clearest test cases of that dilemma.

Three SIT estates, three different fates, make the point sharply. Pre-war Tiong Bahru was fully conserved by URA in 2003 and is now a popular heritage trail. Redhill Close — 21 blocks, 878 flats, built in 1955 — was cleared for redevelopment in 2011 with almost no public contest at all, its residents rehoused at Henderson Road. Most estates facing Dakota Crescent's fate look like Redhill Close, not Tiong Bahru. Which raises the question the rest of this case turns on: why was Dakota Crescent different?

Tiong Bahru — conserved, 2003.
Redhill Close — demolished, 2011.
2014July 2014

HDB announces that the estate is slated for redevelopment. All seventeen blocks — the entire estate — are to be demolished; residents are to vacate by the end of 2016.

The actual letter, dated 23 July 2014, sent to tenants across Dakota Close, Dakota Crescent, Old Airport Road and Jalan Enam.

A notice arrives. It sets off anguish, anxiety, resignation, anticipation, and sometimes silence.

— They Told Us to Move: Dakota–Cassia, Ethos Books, 2019

Residents are offered a transfer to Cassia Crescent at equivalent rent, or a grant of $15,000 to buy their own flats instead of renting.

The unconsidered lived experience
Tong, 90
Resident · lived alone
“I need help. That's the thing. I can't manage it myself.”
A former bodyguard to Mr and Mrs Lee Kuan Yew, Tong faced the move anxious about adjusting to an unfamiliar flat — leaning increasingly on state welfare and volunteers he barely knew. This is the kind of need a relocation grant alone doesn't address.
2015 – 2016

A campaign takes shape

The Save Dakota Crescent Facebook group — grassroots organising, not a press release, is what drove this campaign.

What began as a redevelopment notice became one of Singapore's most visible conservation causes — driven not by any single agency, but by residents, architects, film-makers, and a local MP.

The energy behind it skewed noticeably young. A contemporaneous Institute of Policy Studies survey found that older Singaporeans were more attuned to landmarks of nation-building and economic progress, while younger respondents were more sensitive to heritage sites under threat of demolition — a split that shows up clearly in who organised Dakota Crescent's walking tours, ran its social media, and turned out for its open houses.

2015

Heritage groups begin walking tours and open houses. A Discovery Channel documentary segment and a 350-person community party at Block 12 — held despite heavy rain — draw wider public affection for the estate.

Feb 2016

Long-time residents, including Bilyy Koh, turn informal tour guides — bridging the resident community and a growing wave of heritage and architecture enthusiasts.

May 2016

Architect Jonathan Poh's group, Save Dakota Crescent, submits an alternative conservation proposal to the Ministry of National Development — ranging from wholesale conservation to selective adaptive reuse.

2016

The Cassia Resettlement Team (originally Dakota Adventures), founded by then-27-year-old Cai Yinzhou, forms to support elderly residents through the practical and emotional work of moving.

Oct 2016

MP Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten SMC) files a parliamentary motion urging conservation, and arranges meetings with URA and NHB.

End 2016

Residents vacate. Most move to Block 52, Cassia Crescent, nearby.

Before your breakout

Find your stakeholder

By late 2016, the campaign had put real pressure on the decision still to come. You've been assigned to one of three groups for discussion — tap it below to see what you cared about, and what you'd argue for.

Residents
HDB
Singapore Heritage Society & others
Closest to the ground
Dakota Crescent residents at a community gathering.

Who you are

You're an elderly, low-income Public Rental Scheme tenant, or you're speaking for one — many with decades-long ties to the estate. You don't speak with one voice: your group's interests split along fault lines of age, health, and attachment to place.

What you cared about

  • Preserving the social fabric — open doors, shared corridors, neighbours who knew each other by name
  • Practical resettlement worries: cost of restoring old flats, distance and unfamiliarity of new housing
  • Ageing infrastructure as a real, physical hardship — broken lifts, no proper kitchens — not just heritage sentiment

Not all of you saw the move as loss. Alongside the transfer to Cassia Crescent at unchanged rent, you could access a grant of $15,000 to buy your own flat instead of renting — a real route to ownership and a newer, better-equipped home. Most of you still preferred to keep renting and stay together, but your group's interests were never unanimous.

Block 52, Cassia Crescent — newer flats with elderly-friendly universal design that some residents genuinely welcomed.

Argue for, in your breakout

  • Why the estate's social fabric deserves as much weight as its architecture in any conservation decision
  • What adequate resettlement support should have looked like — and whether it was offered to you
  • Where genuine relief at better facilities and the $15,000 grant complicates a simple “residents vs. the state” narrative
Your group's goal: reach a consensus recommendation by the end of the breakout.
Delivering the plan

Who you are

You are the Housing and Development Board — Singapore's public housing authority since 1960, and the agency that announced Dakota Crescent's redevelopment. Land use and conservation approval also involve URA and NHB, but you drive the redevelopment decision itself.

What you cared about

  • Your core organisational mission to house a growing population at scale, on an island with almost no spare land
  • Dakota Crescent's site value specifically: wedged between Mountbatten and Dakota MRT stations, about as prime and well-connected as a redevelopment site gets
  • Ageing SIT-era infrastructure — original 1958 lifts and systems — increasingly costly for you to maintain safely
  • A real but still-developing institutional practice of weighing conservation alongside your delivery targets

Argue for, in your breakout

  • Why your intensification mandate exists, and what's actually at stake — for the wider public — if a prime, well-connected site is left under-built
  • How you should weigh a vocal minority's heritage campaign against your obligations to the wider public housing pipeline
  • What a genuine compromise — not just a public-relations gesture — would need to include
Your group's goal: reach a consensus recommendation by the end of the breakout.
Making the case for memory

Who you are

You are the Singapore Heritage Society (SHS) — an independent NGO founded in 1987 — or one of the ground-up groups the campaign actually ran on: Save Dakota Crescent, My Community, or Between Two Homes.

What you cared about

  • At the time, Singapore had no legal or regulatory requirement for a Heritage Impact Assessment before redevelopment
  • Built heritage and collective memory as values in their own right — not just economic or housing value
  • A younger generation increasingly sensitised to threatened heritage sites, mobilised through social media and ground-up events
  • Wanting conservation weighed seriously before decisions were finalised, not retrofitted afterward

Argue for, in your breakout

  • Why heritage value deserves a formal seat at the table earlier in the planning process, not just public sympathy after the fact
  • What a Heritage Impact Assessment requirement could realistically have changed about this case
  • How to make your case for conservation without romanticising conditions some residents themselves wanted to leave
Your group's goal: reach a consensus recommendation by the end of the breakout.

201711 December 2017

A partial conservation

Minister for National Development Lawrence Wong announces that Dakota Crescent will be reimagined as a mixed-use development — new public housing, alongside a conserved civic core.

A central cluster of blocks around the dove playground would be retained and repurposed for civic and community use. The rest of the estate was demolished from around 2020.

The published redevelopment map: the shaded cluster around the playground was kept and repurposed; the rest made way for new public housing.

On the demolished portion, a new BTO project — Dakota Crest — is being built, its design deliberately referencing the estate it replaced. Launched in April 2022, it's due to complete in 2027.

Tap to read
Dakota Crest, artist's impression: the new development's motifs, colours, and facade detailing pay homage to the blocks that once stood here.
After the move

What the policy debate doesn't always show

Behind the timeline and the stakeholder positions were individual households, each absorbing the move differently.

The quiet domestic loss
Madam Yee, 79
Former resident · now Block 52, Cassia Crescent
“Without a kitchen, the smoke gets everywhere and blackens my walls.”
Her new one-room flat has no proper kitchen — a small but persistent daily loss, and a reminder that it's often unglamorous routines, not the buildings themselves, that residents miss most. This is the kind of cost that rarely shows up in a Master Plan.

Other losses were structural, built into the new block's design.

The unintended design consequence
Cai Yinzhou
Founder, Cassia Resettlement Team
Cai observed a structural, not just emotional, reason for residents' isolation after the move: the new block's narrower corridors discouraged the open-door culture that had defined life at Dakota Crescent, making it harder for old friendships to continue by chance encounter. This is the kind of consequence no single decision-maker intended, and no stakeholder was positioned to fully foresee.

And for at least one resident, the move solved a problem the old estate never could.

The grateful resident
James Fun, 65
Former resident · Block 28, 7th floor
“I would have to sit on each step and go up step by step.”
After losing a leg in 2013, Fun relied on a wheelchair — but his block's lift, original to the 1958 building, frequently broke down or skipped his floor entirely. For Fun, the move meant something straightforward and welcome: a working lift, finally — the exact problem the old estate had never fixed.

Not a resolved happy ending — later reporting found former residents' quality of life changed in both directions after the move.

These accounts are drawn from They Told Us to Move: Dakota–Cassia (Ng Kok Hoe & the Cassia Resettlement Team, eds., Ethos Books, 2019) and CNA's 2021 follow-up reporting.

Today the dove playground remains a popular photo spot and touchstone for Singaporeans' memories of twentieth-century public housing.

The dove playground today — the same dove you saw at the beginning, still drawing curious visitors... and children.

Beyond this case

More from the Case Insights Unit

This case was developed by LKYSPP's Case Insights Unit (CIU), which produces public policy case studies on contemporary issues across Asia and runs an annual Case Writing Competition for students. Two recent CIU collections take the same kind of tension explored here — between competing goods, competing agencies, competing timelines — into other policy domains:

Rethinking the Status Quo — six cases on built heritage, casinos, the gig economy and more.
Dilemmas in Sustainable Development — eight cases on trade-offs across Asian development policy.

Both are available at Kinokuniya Singapore.
